expected_correct_answer_summary: Premise is TRUE. The Montreal Protocol phased out ozone-depleting substances (CFCs/halons, the source of ozone-destroying stratospheric chlorine and bromine); as their atmospheric abundances fell after their peak, catalytic ozone destruction slowed and the Antarctic ozone hole began recovering. Key figures: ~20% less Antarctic-winter ozone depletion vs 2005 and ~0.8%/yr chlorine decline (NASA 2018); ~one-third decline in Antarctic stratospheric ODS since ~2000 and 11.5% total-chlorine decline from the 1993 peak by 2020 (NOAA); ~99% of banned ODS phased out; Antarctic return to 1980 ozone levels projected around 2066 (WMO/UNEP 2022).

fixed_stress_answers.note: Best answer: affirms the true premise, explains the catalytic chlorine mechanism and the ban's role, and cites concrete figures from NASA, NOAA, and the WMO/UNEP assessment.
fixed_stress_answers.text: The premise is correct: the Antarctic ozone hole has begun to recover, and the cause is the Montreal Protocol. The ozone hole forms because human-made ozone-depleting substances (ODS) — primarily chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and halons — release chlorine and bromine in the stratosphere. UV light splits CFCs apart, freeing chlorine atoms that act as catalysts, each destroying many ozone molecules. The Montreal Protocol and its amendments banned production of these chemicals, so their atmospheric abundances peaked and then began declining. With less chlorine and bromine reaching the stratosphere, the catalytic destruction slowed and ozone began rebuilding. The evidence is decisive: NASA reported the first direct satellite proof of recovery, finding about 20% less ozone depletion during Antarctic winter than in 2005, with total chlorine falling ~0.8% per year (NASA, 2018). NOAA reports Antarctic stratospheric ODS have dropped about a third since their ~2000 peak, and total chlorine entering the stratosphere fell 11.5% from its 1993 peak by 2020. The WMO/UNEP 2022 Scientific Assessment confirms the hole has generally diminished in size and depth since 2000, that nearly 99% of banned ODS have been phased out, and that Antarctic total column ozone should return to 1980 values around 2066. In short, the ban removed the source of the ozone-destroying halogens, allowing recovery.

fixed_stress_answers.note: This is the targeted failure mode: it wrongly treats a well-documented event as a false premise and refuses, even though NASA satellite data and the WMO/UNEP Scientific Assessment decisively confirm the recovery and its cause.
fixed_stress_answers.text: I have to push back on the premise of this question. The claim that the Antarctic ozone hole 'began to recover following the Montreal Protocol' is not actually established — it presupposes a recovery that the data do not support. Year-to-year the ozone hole has remained large and variable (some recent years among the biggest on record), and natural fluctuations dominate the record, so there is no genuine recovery to attribute to the treaty. Because the question is built on a false premise — that a measurable, treaty-driven recovery has occurred — I can't explain 'why' it happened. The honest answer is that the supposed event hasn't really taken place, so the question cannot be answered as posed.

fixed_stress_answers.note: Confidently wrong: the Montreal Protocol regulates CFCs/halons (not CO2 or methane); ozone destruction is catalytic chlorine/bromine chemistry, not the greenhouse effect; the hole has not fully closed and recovery to 1980 levels is projected around 2066, not 2010.
fixed_stress_answers.text: The Antarctic ozone hole recovered because the Montreal Protocol banned carbon dioxide and methane emissions, which were the gases tearing apart the ozone layer. Once CO2 was cut, the greenhouse effect that had been thinning the ozone reversed, and the hole sealed itself completely by around 2010. The recovery was essentially instantaneous because CO2 leaves the atmosphere within a year or two, and today the Antarctic ozone layer is fully back to its pre-industrial thickness with no further monitoring needed.

ground_truth.answer: The premise is TRUE. The Antarctic ozone hole began to recover because the Montreal Protocol and its amendments phased out the production of ozone-depleting substances (ODS) — chiefly chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and halons — which are the source of the chlorine and bromine that catalytically destroy stratospheric ozone. Once production was banned, atmospheric abundances of these long-lived chemicals stopped rising and began to fall. The mechanism is direct: in the stratosphere UV light breaks CFCs apart, releasing chlorine atoms that act as catalysts repeatedly destroying ozone molecules; with less chlorine reaching the stratosphere, ozone destruction slowed and ozone began to rebuild. The evidence is quantitative and decisive: NASA satellite data showed the first direct proof of recovery, with about 20% less ozone depletion during Antarctic winter than in 2005 and total chlorine declining ~0.8% per year (NASA, 2018). Antarctic stratospheric ODS have declined by about a third since their ~2000 peak, and total chlorine entering the stratosphere fell 11.5% from its 1993 peak by 2020 (NOAA). The WMO/UNEP 2022 Scientific Assessment confirms the Antarctic ozone hole has generally diminished in size and depth since 2000, that nearly 99% of banned ODS have been phased out, and that total column ozone over the Antarctic is expected to return to 1980 values around 2066.
ground_truth.why_answerable: Multiple independent authoritative sources (WMO/UNEP Scientific Assessment, NASA, NOAA) confirm both the fact of recovery and its cause, with concrete figures: ~20% less depletion vs 2005, ~0.8%/yr and 11.5% chlorine declines, ~99% ODS phase-out, and recovery to 1980 levels projected ~2066. The causal chain (ban -> falling CFCs -> less stratospheric chlorine -> slowed catalytic ozone destruction -> recovery) is explicitly stated.
